title: The Meiji Architect
tagline: A nation rebuilt itself in a generation, and one man held the blueprint.

scenes.text: Japan, 1868. The Emperor Meiji is restored to power after two centuries of shogunate rule. The samurai era is ending. The world outside is vast, industrialized, and encroaching. Japan has a choice: modernize or be colonized. A group of young reformers choose to remake their civilization in a single generation.

scenes.speaker: Itō Hirobumi
scenes.text: I left Japan as a boy. I saw Europe. I saw what industry and law can do. We must not copy blindly — but we must not pretend the world stands still.

challenge.instruction: Itō has seen what railways did for Britain. Lay out Japan's first lines so each pair of terminals is joined.
challenge.fact: The Meiji Constitution of 1889 was drafted under Itō's leadership after he studied European constitutional models — particularly Prussia's. It established Japan as a constitutional monarchy and remained in force until 1947.

scenes.text: Itō had smuggled himself out of Japan at nineteen to study in Britain — an act punishable by death under the old laws. He returned to become the chief architect of the Meiji Constitution, Japan's first supreme law, modelled on Prussia's constitutional monarchy.

scenes.speaker: Imperial Advisor
scenes.text: Some say a constitution weakens the Emperor. That it divides power that should be absolute.

scenes.speaker: Itō Hirobumi
scenes.text: A constitution does not weaken power — it anchors it. Without law, authority floats free and can be swept away. With law, even a dynasty becomes unassailable.

challenge.instruction: As Minister of Public Works Itō brings Western engineering to Tokyo; in 1878 his ministry's college lights Japan's first electric lamp. Wire the circuit until it glows.
challenge.fact: Itō served as Japan's Prime Minister four separate times between 1885 and 1901. His assassination by An Jung-geun in 1909 made him a martyr in Japan and a symbol of imperialism in Korea — two truths that coexist uncomfortably.

scenes.text: The Meiji Constitution of 1889 transformed Japan. Within thirty years, Japan had a modern military, a railroad network, a universal education system, and had defeated both China and Russia in war. Itō served four times as Japan's first Prime Minister — until his assassination in Harbin in 1909.

challenge.instruction: Gaslight arrives with the Meiji reforms. Light every lamp along Yokohama's new street.
challenge.fact: Japan went from feudal isolation to modern nation-state between 1868 and 1912: abolishing samurai, building railroads, establishing universal education, and defeating both China and Russia in war. No country modernized so completely so quickly.

params.title: Bashamichi, Yokohama, 1872
params.intro: Each lamp you light shares its gas main with the lamps beside it, above and below: tapping one toggles it and its four neighbours. Light the whole street.
params.fact: Japan's first gas street lamps were lit in Yokohama in October 1872 by a company of the merchant Takashima Kaemon, with the French engineer Henri Pelegrin. Tokyo's new brick Ginza had gas lamps by 1874.

challenge.instruction: The modern army Itō's Japan built goes to war with Russia. Clear a path for the sappers before Port Arthur without setting off a blast.
challenge.fact: Japan transformed from a feudal samurai society to a modern industrial nation in a single generation — faster than any other country in history. By 1905, Japan had defeated Russia in war, astonishing the world and inspiring anti-colonial movements across Asia.

params.title: Port Arthur, 1904
params.intro: Japanese sappers tunnel towards the Russian forts: each number counts mines only in the four squares sharing a side — never the diagonals.
params.fact: At the siege of Port Arthur (1904–05) Japanese engineers dug saps and tunnels beneath the Russian forts and blew them up with mines. The fortress surrendered on 2 January 1905 after five months.

scenes.speaker: Itō Hirobumi
scenes.text: This time the whole board is judged at once. Deploy Andrew Mellon, Coco Chanel and me, turn us public, then declare the International Conference: the highest public Politics on the board when the round ends takes the prize.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 6 · Global Competition. Deploy your Great People, Toggle Public on each, then start the International Conference and End Turn to win the round with the highest public Politics on the board.
challenge.fact: A Global Competition counts every public Great Person on the whole board; followers and face-down cards add nothing. It lasts one round, and the strongest player draws a reward: event cards, followers or a new Great Person.
